So the kid is the jury, even though he or she is not being talked to. We've seen presidential debates in large auditoriums where some candidates make the mistake of playing to the jury in the room, trying to get some reaction or trying to get some applause. The real jury is not the 500 people sitting in the room on some college campus for a presidential debate. The real jury would be the millions and millions of people sitting at home watching on television. When I was in court, there would be objections and discussions with judges or between prosecutors and defense attorneys. So if a judge is talking to me, he or she is the audience, right? Not necessarily. Remember, there's a group of 12 sitting off to the side in a jury box, listening to every word that is being said between me and the judge. That was the real jury. That was the audience I was communicating with, even though that is not who I was talking to. Sometimes the jury is more than just who you're talking with. Sometimes the jury is really the group off to the side, listening. That's true in a courtroom. It's true in a boardroom. It's true in a presentation at work. So if you want to be better at expressing yourself and advocating for what you believe and advancing those causes closest to you, I think this book doesn't hurt to ask, can help you. But until then, this is what we need to focus on. What do you believe and why? Are you knowledgeable about the facts, the evidence, the material, the information you need to effectively communicate? Have you vetted that information, tested it, probed it, examined it, cross-examined it to make sure it is accurate and reliable? Have you done the same with the other side of the argument? Do you know it also? Do you know where your weaknesses are? Do you know what your objective is? I mean, do you really, really know what your goal is for that particular interaction?
